name: Tibet (1912-1951)
info: Tibet was a de facto independent state ruled by the Ganden Phodrang government of the Dalai Lamas from the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912 until its annexation by the People's Republic of China in 1951.

facts.founder: The 13th Dalai Lama, who proclaimed independence after the Qing forces were expelled
facts.predecessor: Tibet under Qing rule, the Ganden Phodrang as a Qing protectorate
facts.successor: The People's Republic of China, after the Seventeen Point Agreement of 1951

t: After the Xinhai Revolution the Qing garrison in Lhasa surrendered under the Three Point Agreement, and the 13th Dalai Lama declared that Tibet's relationship with China had ended, though almost no country formally recognised its independence.
The Simla Convention of 1913–1914 between British India, Tibet and the Republic of China was rejected by Beijing, but it defined the McMahon Line between Tibet and India.
In October 1950 the People's Liberation Army entered Chamdo, and in 1951 the Seventeen Point Agreement affirmed China's sovereignty over Tibet.
dyk: Tibet created its own postal service in 1912 and printed its first postage stamps in Lhasa that year, marked "Tibet Government" in Tibetan and "Tibet" in English.
ev: Qing officials in Lhasa signed the Three Point Agreement for the surrender and expulsion of Qing forces from central Tibet
The 13th Dalai Lama returned to Lhasa and issued a proclamation describing Tibet as "a small, religious, and independent nation"
The Simla Convention was initialled by British India, Tibet and China, but Beijing rejected it; McMahon and the Tibetans signed it as a bilateral accord
Lhasa regained control of Chamdo and western Kham, and a truce set the border at the Yangtze River
The armies of Ma Bufang and Liu Wenhui defeated the Tibetan Army in the Sino-Tibetan War
The 13th Dalai Lama died, and China sent a condolence mission to Lhasa headed by General Huang Musong
The 14th Dalai Lama was enthroned in Lhasa on the Tibetan New Year
The People's Liberation Army entered Chamdo, and Tibetan delegates signed the Seventeen Point Agreement in Beijing

sections.foundation:
Tibet had come under the rule of the Qing dynasty in 1720, after the Qing expelled the forces of the Dzungar Khanate, but by the end of the 19th century Qing authority there had become little more than ritual and symbol. In 1910, responding to British encroachment, the Qing sent an expedition to assert greater control. After the Xinhai Revolution of 1911–1912 Tibetan militia attacked the Qing garrison, and the Qing officials in Lhasa were forced to sign the Three Point Agreement for the surrender and expulsion of their forces from central Tibet.

The new Republic of China claimed all the Qing lands, Tibet among them, on the strength of the abdication edict signed by the Empress Dowager Longyu, and its provisional constitution named Tibet an integral part of the state. President Yuan Shikai offered to restore the 13th Dalai Lama's titles; he refused, replying that he intended to exercise both temporal and ecclesiastical rule. Returning to Lhasa in 1913, he proclaimed that the relationship with Beijing had been that of patron and priest. In January 1913 Agvan Dorzhiev signed a treaty with Mongolia in Urga proclaiming mutual recognition.
sections.socioeconomy:
Traditional Tibetan society had a feudal class structure. In the words of Donald S. Lopez, power was monopolised by an elite of a small aristocracy, the hierarchs of the various sects and the great Geluk monasteries. The 13th Dalai Lama had reformed the serf system in the first decade of the 20th century, and by 1950 slavery had probably ceased to exist in central Tibet, though it persisted in places such as the Chumbi Valley, and beggars, the ragyabas, were endemic.

Land was held in hereditary estates, or shiga, granted by the state and revocable, made up of demesne land held by nobles or monasteries and village land held by the central government. Outside the nobility and the monasteries Tibetans were classed as serfs of two kinds: the düchung, bound to corvée labour on estates but holding their own plots and free to move outside their labour periods, and the village tralpa, bound for taxes and transport duties. Half of the village serfs had bought their freedom. A serf absent from his estate for three years became a commoner. The government issued its own banknotes and coins, and from 1912 ran its own postal service.
sections.military:
Once the 13th Dalai Lama had taken full control in the 1910s, he built up the Tibetan Army with British advisers and weapons, meaning it to defend Tibet and to bring in the Tibetan-inhabited lands of Kham. It grew to about 10,000 soldiers by 1936, adequately armed and trained infantry, but it almost entirely lacked machine guns, artillery, aircraft and tanks. Great numbers of poorly armed village militias served beside it. Often outgunned, it fought relatively well against Chinese warlords in the 1920s and 1930s.

In 1918 Lhasa regained Chamdo and western Kham. In 1932 Tibet invaded Qinghai after a dispute over a monastery in Yushu, and the Qinghai and Sichuan armies of Ma Bufang and Liu Wenhui defeated it in the Sino-Tibetan War; the Dalai Lama cabled the British for help and demoted generals who had surrendered. The 1934 Khamba Rebellion led by the Pandatsang family turned Khamba tribesmen against the Tibetan Army. Tibetan troops fought Kazakh refugees entering the plateau in the 1930s and killed the CIA agent Douglas Mackiernan on 29 April 1950. Against the People's Liberation Army in 1950 the army disintegrated and surrendered without much resistance.
sections.governance:
Tibet was governed by the Ganden Phodrang, the government of the Dalai Lamas, with the Kashag as its council of ministers. It was divided into eight chikyaps, each subdivided into dzongs and estates: Lhasa, administering 29 dzongs, Changgyu with its seat at Nagqu, Lhoka at Tsetang, Dakong, Ngari at Gar, Chomo, Shigatse, and Domed or Kham with its seat at Chamdo. Its government controlled Ü-Tsang and Kham west of the Yangtze River, roughly the area of the present Tibet Autonomous Region.

Succession followed the line of incarnations. After the 13th Dalai Lama died in December 1933, Lhamo Dhondup, born in Amdo in 1935, was recognised as his incarnation. On 26 January 1940 the Regent Reting Rinpoche asked the Chinese central government to exempt him from the lot-drawing with the Golden Urn, which it approved, and after a ransom of 400,000 silver dragons was paid to Ma Bufang he travelled to Lhasa and was enthroned at the Potala Palace. Whether Wu Zhongxin presided at the ceremony, as Chinese reports claimed, or was a passive spectator, as the British representative Sir Basil Gould wrote, remains disputed. Tibet set up a Foreign Office in 1942.
sections.impact:
Tibet's status was the subject of rivalry between the British and Russian empires and the Republic of China, and no agreement settled it. The Simla Convention proposed an Outer Tibet, autonomous under Chinese suzerainty, and an Inner Tibet of eastern Kham and Amdo; Beijing rejected it, but the convention drew the McMahon Line, which placed the Tawang tract, administered indirectly through the Tawang monastery, in India. In late 1947 the Tibetan government laid claim to districts south of that line in a note to independent India.

Tibet acted abroad as a state. In 1946 it sent missions to China and India, the first carrying a letter to Chiang Kai-shek that promised to maintain Tibet's independence, and in 1947 a delegation attended the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi, perhaps the first public appearance of the Tibetan national flag. In 1947–49 a trade mission led by Finance Minister Tsepon W. D. Shakabpa visited India, China, Hong Kong, the United States and the United Kingdom, meeting Clement Attlee in 1948, though the countries it visited avoided supporting Tibetan independence. The Austrian Heinrich Harrer, in Lhasa from 1944, tutored the young Dalai Lama.
sections.decline:
China never renounced its claim to Tibet and asserted it at intervals. After 1933 it opened an office in Lhasa under the Mongolian and Tibetan Affairs Commission, and the British opened one of their own. In 1942 Chiang Kai-shek had Ma Bufang repair the Yushu airport, move several thousand troops to the border and threatened the Tibetans with bombing. The same year the United States told Chiang's government that it had never disputed Chinese claims to Tibet.

In 1949, seeing the Communists winning the civil war, the Kashag expelled all Chinese officials from Tibet. On 1 October 1949 the 10th Panchen Lama sent a telegram to Beijing welcoming the coming liberation of Tibet, and the government of Mao Zedong soon moved to reassert Chinese presence. In June 1950 Britain said it would recognise Chinese suzerainty only if Tibet were regarded as autonomous. In October 1950 the People's Liberation Army entered Chamdo, defeating sporadic resistance. In 1951 a delegation headed by Ngapoi Ngawang Jigme, with the Dalai Lama's authorisation, negotiated in Beijing the Seventeen Point Agreement affirming China's sovereignty; it was ratified in Lhasa months later, and China called it the "peaceful liberation of Tibet".

summary: Between the fall of the Qing in 1912 and the Seventeen Point Agreement of 1951, Tibet under the 13th and 14th Dalai Lamas governed itself, kept its own army, currency, post and foreign office, and called itself independent, while China maintained its claim and almost no state recognised Tibetan independence. The People's Liberation Army's advance in 1950 ended it.

pointDescs.1912: The Qing garrison in central Tibet surrendered and was expelled under the Three Point Agreement; Tibet set up its own postal service.
pointDescs.1913: The 13th Dalai Lama returned to Lhasa and proclaimed Tibet a small, religious and independent nation; a treaty with Mongolia was signed at Urga.
pointDescs.1914: The Simla Convention was rejected by Beijing but signed by McMahon and the Tibetans as a bilateral accord drawing the McMahon Line.
pointDescs.1918: Lhasa regained Chamdo and western Kham, and a truce set the border at the Yangtze River.
pointDescs.1932: The Tibetan Army, invading Qinghai, was defeated by Ma Bufang and Liu Wenhui in the Sino-Tibetan War.
pointDescs.1933: The 13th Dalai Lama died in December, and China sent a condolence mission to Lhasa.
pointDescs.1936: The Tibetan Army, built up with British advice and weapons, numbered about 10,000 soldiers.
pointDescs.1940: The 14th Dalai Lama was enthroned at the Potala Palace on the Tibetan New Year.
pointDescs.1947: A Tibetan delegation attended the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi, and a trade mission under Tsepon W. D. Shakabpa set out abroad.
pointDescs.1949: The Kashag expelled all Chinese officials from Tibet as the Communists won the civil war.
pointDescs.1950: The People's Liberation Army entered Chamdo in October and the Tibetan Army surrendered without much resistance.
pointDescs.1951: The Seventeen Point Agreement, negotiated in Beijing and ratified in Lhasa, affirmed China's sovereignty over Tibet.

notes: The article's reference lists were not saved (headings only), so references are empty.
Tibet's status is contested: the text states Tibet's claims and China's claims as the article attributes them; the 1940 enthronement dispute (Wu Zhongxin presiding or not) is given both ways.
The article's Government section is empty; the governance section rests on the administrative divisions, the Kashag mentions and the succession of 1940.
The 1936 point (army of 10,000) is a strength marker from the military section, not an event.
